1191.title: Mimamsa (ritual as meaning)
1191.hook: eat your spinach, the sailor got strong: Mimamsa's rule for the stories that sit beside a command
1191.howItsDone: Mimamsa readers sort the Veda into injunctions and supporting passages, arthavada, and read the praise and stories as serving the acts they stand beside, so that these passages have a purpose.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mimamsa called the Veda apaurusheya: words with no author, and a bond of word and meaning nobody invented.

Eat your spinach. The kid at the table pushes it around the plate. So the parent tries again. You know the cartoon sailor? One can of spinach and he could lift a ship. The kid looks at the spinach differently now. The story about the sailor isn't a history lesson. Nobody's checking whether sailors really work that way. It's there for one reason: to make the instruction land. Mimamsa found the Veda doing the same thing, and it made a rule about it.
screen: `EAT YOUR SPINACH.` → `THE CARTOON SAILOR.` → `THE STORY SERVES THE COMMAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the problem Jaimini faced. Mimamsa says the Veda is about dharma, what is to be done. But parts of the Veda don't tell anyone to do anything. They praise, they explain, they tell stories about the gods. So in the second section of his first book, Jaimini lets an objector speak. If the Veda's purpose is action, the objector says, these passages that ask for nothing have no purpose at all. Shabara's commentary gives an example the objector might point to, a passage that simply tells of a god who wept. Jaimini's answer is the rule. These passages, called arthavada, belong together with the injunctions they stand beside. They have a purpose: they praise the act that's being asked for. They are the sailor and his spinach. A story about the gods, set next to a command, makes the command shine. So, in Jaimini's answer, these passages aren't wasted. They help the asking. This is one more sense of our title, ritual as meaning. Mimamsa reads everything, even the stories, as pointing to something done. And that's our last day with Mimamsa: the desire to know dharma, dharma heard in injunction, not seen by the eye, apurva carrying the act to its fruit, words with no author, and stories in the service of the doing. Next, a school reads many of the same texts with a different question in mind, and we'll hear it on its own terms.
screen: `PASSAGES THAT ASK FOR NOTHING.` · `ARTHAVADA PRAISES THE ACT.` · `NO LINE IS WASTED.` · `EVEN STORIES POINT TO DOING.`

segments.voice: Choose one plain action, bringing your palms together, then laying them open on your knees, and do it once, carefully, in order, with full attention. Rest, then do it again exactly the same way, without explaining it to yourself, and let the doing be enough. If you pray, you can make that small movement your offering.
Mimamsa. The school that reads the Veda as instruction, where even the stories, arthavada, are there to praise the act that's asked for.
Your line: Mimamsa, ritual as meaning. Even the stories point to something done. Until tomorrow.

1192.title: Vedanta (revisited)
1192.hook: the Brahma Sutra's first word is now, and its great commentators stop to ask: now, after what?
1192.howItsDone: Students of Vedanta traditionally begin the Brahma Sutra with its first line, the wish to know Brahman, and read it alongside a teacher's commentary, often Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, depending on their lineage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Mimamsa: arthavada, stories that praise the act being asked for.

Now. It's a small word, and hardly anyone stops on it. A coach says, now we run. A teacher says, now open your books. Nobody asks: now, after what? Vedanta's root text, the Brahma Sutra, opens almost the way Mimamsa's does: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman, where Mimamsa had dharma. Tradition calls Mimamsa the earlier inquiry and Vedanta the later one. We met Vedanta before, in other seasons; this week it comes back as one of the six ways of seeing. And its great commentators stop on that first small word.

Mimamsa asked: what is to be done? Its answer was the act, done rightly, as the Veda directs. Vedanta keeps the same seriousness and turns it toward a different question: what is, underneath everything that is done? Tradition reads the name Vedanta as the Veda's end, and it points to the Upanishads, the teachings that close the Vedic texts. So the later inquiry starts where the hymns and the rituals leave off. Then that small first word: now. Now, after what? The great commentators stop on it, and they don't agree. Shankara says the now comes after a person has learned to tell the lasting from the passing, has cooled toward rewards in this world and the next, has gathered calm and self-control, and longs to be free. For him, the readiness is in the person. Ramanuja reads it another way. For him, the now comes after the study of ritual, after Mimamsa itself. The earlier inquiry prepares the ground, and the later one builds on it. Two teachers, one word, two honest readings, and the tradition keeps both on the shelf. What they share is the word wish. The Sutra doesn't open with a claim. It opens with wanting to know. Vedanta starts the way a good question starts: with someone who has done the things, kept the days, lit the lamps, and still wants to know what all of it rests on.
screen: `WHAT IS TO BE DONE? WHAT IS?` · `THE VEDA'S END: THE UPANISHADS.` · `NOW, AFTER WHAT? TWO READINGS.` · `IT OPENS WITH WANTING TO KNOW.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly what had to happen first for you to be sitting here, the day you've had, the people, the small choices, and let them pass without sorting them. Then let one question rise that's really yours, about what your life rests on, and don't answer it; hold the wanting to know the way you'd hold a warm cup. If you pray, you can rest in the presence of the One you pray to while you hold it.
Vedanta. The later inquiry: it takes Mimamsa's seriousness about the act and asks what everything rests on. Today's word.
Your line: Vedanta, revisited. It opens not with a claim but with wanting to know. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1193.title: Vedanta (revisited)
1193.hook: a thin new moon, a tree branch, and the Brahma Sutra's second line: you can point at what you can't hold
1193.howItsDone: In traditional Vedanta study, teachers explain the Brahma Sutra's second line alongside Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1 and 2.1, and they often use the image of showing the moon through a tree branch to explain how a definition can point rather than describe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vedanta opened its book with a wish: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman.
screen: `THE WISH TO KNOW.` · `THEN WHAT IS IT?`

segments.voice: It's dusk, and a parent is crouched beside a small child, pointing at the sky. The new moon is up, a thin curve, almost nothing. The child can't find it. So the parent tries again. See that tree? See the top branch? Right above it. And suddenly the child sees. Nobody thinks the moon is sitting on the branch. The branch was only a way of getting the eyes to the right place. Vedanta teachers call this the branch-and-moon way, and it explains the Brahma Sutra's second line, the one that tries to say what Brahman is.
screen: `A THIN NEW MOON.` → `SEE THAT BRANCH?` → `THE BRANCH ONLY POINTS.`

segments.voice: The Sutra opened by wanting to know Brahman. So the obvious next question is: what is Brahman? The second line answers, but not the way you might expect. It says, in effect: that from which the birth and so on of this world come. Birth, staying, and dissolving. Brahman is that from which all of it arises, by which it lasts, into which it goes. That's a branch, not a moon. It doesn't describe Brahman. It points from things you know, a world being born and fading, toward their source. The line leans on the Taittiriya Upanishad, where a father gives his son nearly the same pointer: seek that from which these beings are born. We followed that son, Bhrigu, in an earlier year. Here it becomes a definition. Vedanta teachers say there are two ways to say what something is. One is by a mark that belongs to the thing itself. The other is by a mark that only points, like the branch. The Taittiriya gives the first kind too, in another line: Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite. But even there, some readers, Shankara among them, hear pointing. Truth, so not false. Knowledge, so not dull matter. Infinite, so not this one thing or that one. When a tradition points instead of describing, it isn't being vague. It's being careful. Some things you reach by following a gesture, not by holding a picture.
screen: `THAT FROM WHICH THE WORLD ARISES.` · `A POINTER, NOT A PORTRAIT.` · `TRUTH, KNOWLEDGE, THE INFINITE.` · `CAREFUL, NOT VAGUE.`

segments.voice: Notice one breath arriving and ask, without words if you can, where it comes from; notice it staying, then leaving, and ask where it goes. Let the breath be the branch and rest your attention just past it, in the quiet it rises from and returns to, letting any picture go. If you pray, you can let the breath carry a name you hold dear.
Vedanta. Today, its way of pointing: Brahman as that from which the world is born, by which it lasts, into which it returns. Today's word.

1194.title: Vedanta (revisited)
1194.hook: a father's short line to his son, "you are that", and three great teachers who hear it three ways
1194.howItsDone: Hindus in the Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita lines each study the Upanishads through their own teacher's commentary, Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, and the line tat tvam asi is read and taught in each lineage in its own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vedanta pointed: Brahman as that from which the world is born, like a branch showing the moon.
screen: `THE BRANCH AND THE MOON.` · `ONE LINE, THREE HEARINGS.`

segments.voice: Tat tvam asi. You are that. A father says it to his son in the Chandogya Upanishad, again and again, after showing him salt dissolved in water and a seed split open to nothing you can see. And here is the surprise. Three of Vedanta's great teachers, Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva, each honor this line and build on it, and they don't hear it the same way. Same words, same Upanishad, same Brahma Sutra underneath. Today each of the three reads the line aloud.
screen: `TAT TVAM ASI.` → `ONE LINE EVERYONE HONORS.` → `THREE TEACHERS AT ONE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Shankara reads it straight. You, at your deepest, are Brahman. Not part of it, not near it. Advaita teaching offers an image: the sense of being a separate little self is like the space inside a clay pot. Break the pot and nothing goes anywhere; the space was never two. His school is called Advaita, not-two. Ramanuja reads the same line and keeps the self real. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya speaks of the one who dwells within all things, whom the things don't know, whose body they are, who guides them from inside. For Ramanuja, that's the key. The world and every self are like Brahman's body. A body is truly real, truly yours, and never apart from you. So you are that, the way a body belongs wholly to the one who lives in it. His school is called Vishishtadvaita. Madhva reads the line and hears difference. For him, Brahman, whom he knows as Vishnu, and the self are always two, and the self is wholly dependent, like a reflection that's real, but only because something shines. The line, read his way, speaks of closeness and likeness, never sameness. His school is called Dvaita, two. Three readings, each one argued with care from the same texts. Hindus who follow each line keep reading, praying and living by it to this day. The darshanas are never ranked here, and neither are these.
screen: `SHANKARA: NEVER TWO.` · `RAMANUJA: THE WORLD AS GOD'S BODY.` · `MADHVA: ALWAYS TWO, ALWAYS CLOSE.` · `THREE READINGS, NONE RANKED.`

segments.voice: Let the words come quietly, you are that, and hear them first as Shankara might, resting as the open space the pot never divided; then as Ramanuja might, feeling yourself held from inside, the way a body belongs to the one who lives in it; then as Madhva might, noticing that you didn't make yourself shine. Give each a few breaths, and you don't have to choose. If you pray, you can let the line rest in the name you pray to.
Vedanta. Today, the line you are that, heard as not-two, as body and soul, and as two who stay close. Today's word.
Your line: Vedanta, revisited. One line, three readings, none ranked. Same time tomorrow.

1195.title: Vedanta (revisited)
1195.hook: how do you start a new school of thought without a new scripture? in Vedanta, you write on the books everyone already shares
1195.howItsDone: In Vedanta lineages, a teacher's standing rests on commentary: students read the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutra through their own school's commentaries, and the founders of the major schools each commented on the Brahma Sutra and the Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vedanta, one line, you are that, heard three ways: not-two, body and soul, two who stay close.

Say you have a new insight about the deepest things, and you're sure of it. How do you get anyone to take it seriously? You could announce a new book. You could gather followers. In Vedanta, the answer is quieter and much harder. You sit down with the books everybody already reads, the ones your rivals read too, and you go through them line by line, showing how your insight was there all along. Yesterday's three teachers didn't each bring their own scripture. They wrote commentaries on the same shelf.
screen: `A NEW INSIGHT.` → `NO NEW BOOK.` → `WRITE ON THE SHARED SHELF.`

segments.voice: Tradition names the shelf the prasthanas, the starting points, and it names them together. The Upanishads, the teachings at the end of the Veda, which tradition counts as shruti, what was heard. The Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna on the battlefield, part of the Mahabharata, a text of smriti, what was remembered. And the Brahma Sutra, the short, packed lines that try to gather what the Upanishads teach and answer objections. Tradition describes them as a starting point in revelation, one in remembered teaching, and one in reasoning. Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva each wrote a commentary on the Brahma Sutra and on the Gita, and each read the Upanishads closely. That's how a Vedanta school stands up: by showing that its reading makes sense of the shared texts, all of them, including the hard verses. The Brahma Sutra itself says why this matters. Early on, it says, in effect, that Brahman is known from the Upanishads because they all fit together around it. The texts aren't a pile. They're meant to agree. So every teacher's task is to show the agreement, and the arguments between the schools are arguments about how the pieces fit. There's something generous in that. Nobody gets to win by changing the subject. You stay with the same pages your neighbor reads, and you keep reading until you can say, here, this is what I see.
screen: `THE STARTING POINTS.` · `HEARD, REMEMBERED, REASONED.` · `EVERY SCHOOL WRITES ON THE SAME SHELF.` · `THE TEXTS ARE MEANT TO AGREE.`

segments.voice: Let one line you know and love come to mind, a verse, a song, something someone wise once told you, and say it inwardly, slowly. Ask what's here that you haven't seen before, and instead of hunting for a clever answer, let the line sit and see what it shows you when you stay. If you pray, you can hold that line as an offering.
Vedanta. Today, its shared shelf: the Upanishads, the Gita, the Brahma Sutra, and every school showing how they fit. Today's word.
Your line: Vedanta, revisited. Every school writes on the same shelf, and none wins by changing the subject. Until tomorrow.

1196.title: Vedanta (revisited)
1196.hook: the Brahma Sutra opens with "now" and closes by saying the same words twice: no return, no return

1196.howItsDone: Traditional students of the Brahma Sutra read it from its first line to its last, the repeated words 'no return', usually through their own lineage's commentary, Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vedanta's shared shelf: the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutra, with every school writing on the same pages.

The Brahma Sutra ends by saying the same thing twice. After all its packed little lines, the arguments, the objections, the answers, the very last words are: no return, on the word of scripture. No return, on the word of scripture. Tradition reads the doubling as a way of signaling the end, like a bell rung a second time so everyone knows the music is over. The book opened with its first word, now. With its last line, we close our visit to Vedanta.
screen: `THE SAME WORDS TWICE.` → `NO RETURN, NO RETURN.` → `FROM NOW TO THE LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: No return from what? The last part of the Brahma Sutra is about the one who has come to know Brahman, and what happens when this life ends. The answer is that such a one does not come back into the turning of birth and death. And notice what the line rests its case on: the word of scripture. It's leaning on the Chandogya Upanishad, whose closing lines say of the one who reaches the world of Brahman: he does not return, he does not return. The Sutra ends by echoing the Upanishad's own ending. The book that set out to gather the Upanishads finishes in their voice. And then, true to this week, the schools fill in what no return means in their own ways. For Shankara, freedom is knowing what was always so: the self was never anything but Brahman, and nothing needs to travel anywhere. For Ramanuja and for Madhva, the freed self stays itself and lives in the presence of the Lord, whom they know as Vishnu, in a joy that doesn't end. Each reading is argued from these same lines. Now set the first word beside the last. Now: the wish to know. No return: the wish fulfilled. Vedanta, as a darshana, is a way of seeing the whole of life as that kind of journey, from a real question to an answer that doesn't need to be asked again.
screen: `NO RETURN TO BIRTH AND DEATH.` · `ECHOING THE CHANDOGYA'S ENDING.` · `EACH SCHOOL FILLS IN NO RETURN.` · `FROM THE WISH TO THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing that's done, a task, a conversation, a worry already resolved, and notice how it keeps circling back anyway. Breathe out and let it not return, then let it go a second time, gently, the way the Sutra says its last words twice, and rest in whatever is left. If you pray, you can hand it over to the One you pray to.
Vedanta. From the first word, now, the wish to know, to the last, no return, said twice. Today's word, and the last of our visit with it.
Your line: Vedanta, revisited. From the wish to know to an answer that needn't be asked again. Rest well.

1197.howItsDone: Students of Indian philosophy traditionally study the six darshanas in pairs, Nyaya with Vaisheshika, Samkhya with Yoga, and Mimamsa with Vedanta, and Hindus also use the word darshana for seeing the deity at a temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vedanta's last line, no return, said twice, closed the book that opened with now.
screen: `VEDANTA: NOW TO NO RETURN.` · `A WEEK TO LOOK BACK ON.`

segments.voice: You're sitting in the eye doctor's chair, chin on the rest, a heavy metal frame in front of your face. Click. Better like this? Click. Or like this? The letters on the wall don't change. What changes is how they come to you. Some lenses make the top line sharp and the bottom line a blur. Nobody in that chair thinks the lenses are fighting each other. They're tools for seeing. We've walked through the six darshanas, the classical schools of Hindu thought. Now we start using them that way: each one as a lens.
screen: `CLICK. BETTER LIKE THIS?` → `THE LETTERS DON'T CHANGE.` → `SIX SCHOOLS, SIX LENSES.`

segments.voice: Start with the word itself. Darshana means a view, a way of seeing. It's the same word Hindus use at the temple, for seeing the deity and being seen. So a school of thought, in this tradition, is named for an act of looking. Behind us: Mimamsa read the ritual act as meaning. Then Vedanta, revisited: a book that opens with the wish to know Brahman, a definition that points like a branch at the moon, one line, you are that, heard three ways, a shared shelf every school writes on, and a last line said twice. Now step back. One way to hold the six schools is by the question each one keeps asking. Nyaya asks: how do I know? Vaisheshika asks: what is this made of? Samkhya asks: who is watching? Yoga asks: what is the mind doing right now? Mimamsa asks: what is this act for? Vedanta asks: what does all of it rest on? Those are our short versions, not the schools' own words. But each one is a real lens. Click one in and certain things go sharp. Over the next few days we'll try them two at a time, on ordinary moments: a rumor, a flash of anger, a sink full of dishes. Then comes the invitation in the title. Each as a lens for a week. Not to choose a winner. This part of the path is called schools of thought, never ranked, and that's the rule we keep.
screen: `DARSHANA: A WAY OF SEEING.` · `THE WEEK: MIMAMSA AND VEDANTA.` · `SIX SCHOOLS, SIX QUESTIONS.` · `LENSES, NOT RIVALS.`

segments.voice: Choose something simple, the feeling of sitting where you are, and ask it each question once, without answering in words: how do I know I'm sitting, what is this made of, who is noticing, what is the mind doing, what is this for, what does it rest on? Then let the questions go and just sit, seen without any lens at all. If you pray, you can offer the moment as it is.
Each as a lens for a week. The six darshanas, held not as rivals, but as ways of seeing you can try on one at a time. Today's word.
